explanation: The fourth ventricle is the cavity of the hindbrain (rhombencephalon), communicates with third ventricle above and subarachnoid space below via median/lateral apertures, and has a roof and floor.
CSF reaches the cisterna magna via the foramen of Magendie (fourth ventricle directly to subarachnoid space), NOT through the aqueduct of Sylvius (which connects third and fourth ventricles).
MCA supplies auditory area, Broca's area, and frontal eye field; the whole primary motor area (for face and hand) is supplied by MCA, not an exception; the leg area is ACA.

Middle cerebral artery does NOT directly participate in the circle of Willis; it arises from the internal carotid as a branch outside the circle. The circle includes ACA, PCA, ICA, and posterior communicating arteries.
ACA supplies the paracentral lobule (motor and sensory for lower limb), medial aspect of frontal/parietal lobes; auditory cortex is supplied by MCA, not ACA.

The matching pairs are: Posterior cerebral winds round crus cerebri; Circulus arteriosus (circle of Willis) is in interpeduncular fossa; Basilar lies in median pontine groove; Anterior cerebral runs above corpus callosum; Middle cerebral lies in lateral sulcus.
Anterior cerebral artery central branches supply anterior portions of caudate nucleus and lentiform nucleus, forming lenticulostriate arteries that also supply internal capsule.
Upper half of internal capsule is supplied by central branches of anterior cerebral artery; lower half receives branches from anterior choroidal and posterior communicating arteries.
Vertebrobasilar system supplies cerebellum, inner ear (labyrinthine artery), occipital cortex (PCA), and pons; the temporal pole is supplied by MCA, not vertebrobasilar.

MCA cortical branches supply lateral part of orbital surface, lateral surface (most except occipital), and temporal pole; occipital lobe and paracentral lobule are supplied by PCA and ACA respectively.
PCA supplies: occipital lobe (visual cortex), lower border of temporal lobe, thalamus (central branches), and posterior limb of internal capsule; all of these are correct.
Central branches of PCA (thalamogeniculate arteries) supply thalamus, lateral/genual geniculate bodies, and posterior parts of caudate and lentiform nuclei.
The superficial middle cerebral vein drains into the cavernous sinus; superior and inferior cerebral veins drain into superior sagittal and transverse sinuses respectively.
The great cerebral vein (of Galen) receives internal cerebral veins and drains into the straight sinus; internal cerebral vein drains deep structures into great cerebral vein.
The brain absolutely requires glucose and oxygen at all times; it cannot use fatty acids as an energy source and depends almost exclusively on glucose oxidation for ATP production.
In fasting, brain glucose comes from hepatic glycogenolysis (immediately) and gluconeogenesis from lactate, amino acids, and glycerol (sustained); intestine is not a source during fasting.
Brain cells uptake glucose via GLUT1 (blood-brain barrier) and GLUT3 (neurons); GLUT2 is in liver/pancreas, GLUT4 is insulin-dependent in muscle/adipose.
Brain glucose uptake is insulin-independent; GLUT1 and GLUT3 are constitutively active at the blood-brain barrier and neuronal membranes, ensuring constant glucose supply.

Brain cells completely oxidize glucose to CO2 and H2O via aerobic metabolism in mitochondria, producing 30-32 ATP per glucose molecule; they do not produce lactate or ketone bodies under normal conditions.
Brain uses hexokinase (not glucokinase) to phosphorylate glucose, giving it high affinity for glucose and allowing uptake even at low blood glucose concentrations.
Glucose 6-phosphate in brain cells enters glycolysis; the pentose phosphate pathway also operates for nucleotide synthesis, but glycolysis is the main utilization pathway.
